points: Work samples 0.34, assessment centers 0.37, integrity 0.41

cards.front: What is the validity of job knowledge tests, and what's the book's typo?
cards.answer: 0.48. Table 6.3 prints '.048', which is a typo for 0.48.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.7 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.7 Assessment Methods; 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Erratum: the decimal point is misplaced in the book
Job knowledge tests predict well, especially for complex jobs

cards.front: Which assessment methods tend to have moderate adverse impact?
cards.answer: Cognitive ability tests and interviews (structured and unstructured).
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.7 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.7 Assessment Methods
points: Most other methods are rated low; medical/background checks are mixed

cards.front: What are the most common résumé lies?
cards.answer: Overstated skill mastery, stretched tenure to hide an employer, and a false reason for leaving.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.8 Screening Assessment Methods
points: 2020 Checkster survey of 400 applicants and 400 managers
A signed 'falsification means termination' statement improves honesty

cards.front: Which Yahoo CEO left in 2012 over a padded résumé?
cards.answer: Scott Thompson. The book wrongly names Ross Levinsohn, who was his interim replacement.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.8 Screening Assessment Methods
points: Erratum: teach Thompson; know the book says Levinsohn
Lesson: verify self-reported credentials

cards.front: Why use a job application in addition to a résumé?
cards.answer: It gathers the same information from everyone, making comparison easier and checking résumé accuracy.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.8 Screening Assessment Methods
points: Include: inaccurate information is grounds for dismissal
Keep demographic questions away from recruiters

cards.front: What does a telephone screen typically confirm?
cards.answer: Résumé facts, availability, salary expectations, deal-breakers, and willingness to relocate or travel.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.8 Screening Assessment Methods
points: Can also probe culture fit and other suitable positions

cards.front: What do cognitive ability tests measure, and how well do they predict?
cards.answer: General mental ability (reasoning, logic, perception); they predict success in virtually all jobs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.9 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.9 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Cognitive and Noncognitive Ability Tests
points: Most important for complex jobs, newcomers, and jobs requiring new learning
Examples: Wonderlic, Raven's Progressive Matrices

cards.front: What is the main risk of cognitive ability tests, and how do you manage it?
cards.answer: They tend to produce disparate impact, so never use them alone; combine them with other assessments.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.9 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.9 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Cognitive and Noncognitive Ability Tests
points: Combining keeps prediction while reducing adverse impact
Applicants dislike them as not job-related

cards.front: What do noncognitive ability tests measure?
cards.answer: Sensory abilities (seeing, hearing, speech) and psychomotor abilities (strength, dexterity, coordination).
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.9 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.9 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Cognitive and Noncognitive Ability Tests
points: Physical tests must be truly job-necessary; they can cause adverse impact

cards.front: What are the Big Five personality traits?
cards.answer: Extraversion, conscientiousness, emotional stability, agreeableness, and openness to experience.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.10 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.10 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Personality and Values Assessments and Integrity Tests
points: Text: they capture up to 75% of personality
Not predictive enough to use alone

cards.front: Which Big Five trait predicts performance in all occupations?
cards.answer: Conscientiousness: planful, detail-oriented, rule-following, and hardworking.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.10 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.10 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Personality and Values Assessments and Integrity Tests
points: Emotional stability predicts most jobs
Together they're the 'will do' factors; cognitive ability is 'can do'

cards.front: What does each of the other Big Five traits predict?
cards.answer: Extraversion: sales and management. Agreeableness: teamwork and helping. Openness: creativity and expat success.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.10 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.10 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Personality and Values Assessments and Integrity Tests
points: These predict only for specific jobs or criteria

cards.front: What legal caution applies to personality testing?
cards.answer: Questions that reveal a mental impairment or psychological condition may violate the ADA.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.10 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.10 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Personality and Values Assessments and Integrity Tests
points: Protect test scores; consult a lawyer

cards.front: What do integrity tests measure, and what are their strengths?
cards.answer: Honesty, reliability, and trustworthiness; low adverse impact, cheap, and they predict theft and misconduct.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.10 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.10 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Personality and Values Assessments and Integrity Tests
points: Unrelated to cognitive ability, so they add prediction
Most useful for cash handling, in-home work, valuables

cards.front: What do job knowledge tests measure?
cards.answer: Job-related, often technical, knowledge of duties, tools, and processes.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Example: an HR knowledge test for an HR applicant
Minimal adverse impact; predict well for complex jobs

cards.front: Why do employers and applicants like interviews?
cards.answer: They assess interpersonal skills and leadership, seem job-related, and double as recruiting.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: They also let candidates self-select out

cards.front: What is an unstructured interview?
cards.answer: One where questions vary by candidate and there are no standards for judging answers.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Relies on personal theories (eye contact, appearance) and gut judgment
Hard to compare, weak prediction, expensive, legally risky: not recommended

cards.front: Why are unstructured interviews not recommended?
cards.answer: Answers are hard to compare, they predict poorly, and they're expensive and legally risky.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews; 6.7 Assessment Methods
points: Validity only 0.20-0.38

cards.front: What are the three features of a structured interview?
cards.answer: Same questions for everyone, questions built from a job analysis, and a formal scoring system.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Trained raters use predetermined scoring keys
Reduces bias from attractiveness and other irrelevant factors

cards.front: What are the trade-offs of a structured interview?
cards.answer: It predicts well and reduces bias, but it costs more and requires interviewer training.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Validity 0.51-0.63

cards.front: What are the two types of structured interview?
cards.answer: Behavioral (past behavior) and situational (hypothetical scenarios).
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Both can be mixed in one interview

cards.front: What is a behavioral interview?
cards.answer: A structured interview asking how the candidate actually handled past situations, since past behavior predicts future.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Candidate describes situation, action, result
Cue: 'Tell me about a time...'

cards.front: Which candidates are behavioral interviews best suited for?
cards.answer: Experienced candidates who have relevant past situations to describe.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Train scorers, ask consistently, probe skillfully

cards.front: What is a situational interview?
cards.answer: A structured interview posing hypothetical scenarios and asking what the candidate would do.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Cue: 'What would you do if...' or 'How would you handle...'
Southwest Airlines uses them

cards.front: Which candidates are situational interviews best suited for?
cards.answer: Candidates with limited work experience, since no past examples are needed.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Predicts well

cards.front: What is a case interview?
cards.answer: Giving the candidate a business problem to solve and present, thinking aloud.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Candidate may ask questions; rarely one right answer
Common in consulting and investment banking

cards.front: What does a case interview assess?
cards.answer: Business knowledge, reasoning, presentation, and communication; the process matters more than the answer.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: That's why candidates should think aloud

cards.front: How do structured, behavioral, and case interviews differ?
cards.answer: Structured = same scored questions; behavioral = real past actions; case = solve a business problem aloud.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Behavioral is one type of structured interview; situational is the other
Case focuses on the reasoning process

cards.front: What is the quickest cue for labeling an interview question?
cards.answer: Past = behavioral; hypothetical = situational; business problem = case; no standards = unstructured.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Same questions plus scoring key = structured

cards.front: How do structured interview rating scales work?
cards.answer: Answers are scored against anchors, e.g., 5 = empathize and solve, 3 = apologize and refund, 1 = call manager.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Anchors make scoring consistent across interviewers

cards.front: What is the bias concern with AI interview tools like HireVue?
cards.answer: Algorithms can be blind to protected traits, but correlated features must be checked and mitigated.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews
points: Human implicit and explicit bias also causes adverse impact

cards.front: What are work samples?
cards.answer: Assessments of performance on actual or simulated job tasks, from judgment questions to portfolios.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.12 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.12 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Work Samples and Interviews (Work Samples & Assessment Centers)
points: Low adverse impact, well received, hard to fake
Expensive; best for short tasks

cards.front: What is a simulation in selection?
cards.answer: A work sample that gives real tasks or recreates critical job events.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.12 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.12 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Work Samples and Interviews (Work Samples & Assessment Centers)
points: Example: a 911 call-taker handling mock calls
Validity 0.54

cards.front: What is an assessment center?
cards.answer: A battery of exercises (in-basket, group discussion, role-plays, presentations) scored by trained assessors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.12 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.12 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Work Samples and Interviews (Work Samples & Assessment Centers)
points: About 6 participants; can last days
Report covers strengths, development needs, overall potential

cards.front: What is an in-basket exercise?
cards.answer: Handling a stack of memos and tasks under a time limit, as in an assessment center.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.12 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.12 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Work Samples and Interviews (Work Samples & Assessment Centers)
points: Tests prioritizing and decision making

cards.front: Why do employers check references even though former employers say little?
cards.answer: Documented reference checks reduce negligent hiring risk and can still confirm key facts.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.13 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.13 Contingent Assessment Methods: Reference Checks and Medical and Drug Tests
points: Former employers fear defamation claims
Ask about fit and behavior, not just dates

cards.front: When may an employer require a medical exam?
cards.answer: Only after a contingent offer, for everyone entering the job, if job-related and a business necessity.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.13 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.13 Contingent Assessment Methods: Reference Checks and Medical and Drug Tests
points: ADA rule; keep results confidential and stored separately
Collected last so the reason for any rejection is clear

cards.front: What should a drug-testing policy tell applicants in advance?
cards.answer: Who's tested, which substances, timing, cutoff levels, confirmation steps, safeguards, and consequences.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.13 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.13 Contingent Assessment Methods: Reference Checks and Medical and Drug Tests
points: Drug tests are the most common medical test
Know state rules and union contracts

cards.front: What does the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) require?
cards.answer: Applicants get a copy of their credit report and a rights summary, with a chance to fix errors first.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.14 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.14 Contingent Assessment Methods: Background Checks
points: About half of employers run credit checks; critics call them unfair

cards.front: What are 'ban the box' laws?
cards.answer: Laws delaying criminal-history questions until after initial qualification, or a conditional offer for federal jobs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.14 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.14 Contingent Assessment Methods: Background Checks
points: Records disproportionately affect Black and Hispanic applicants
35+ states and 150 cities/counties by 2020

cards.front: What is an adverse action notice?
cards.answer: Notice of negative background information, with the screener's contact details and the right to dispute it.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.14 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.14 Contingent Assessment Methods: Background Checks
points: Allow fair time to contest

cards.front: How should employers evaluate a criminal record?
cards.answer: Individually: the nature and gravity of the offense, time since it occurred, and the nature of the job.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.14 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.14 Contingent Assessment Methods: Background Checks
points: Checks must be job-relevant, disclosed, consented to in writing, and documented

cards.front: What makes MITRE's hiring process a good example?
cards.answer: It's transparent and courteous: every résumé is acknowledged and every step is published.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.15 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.15 Case Study: Hiring at MITRE Corporation
points: Up to 3 months; 2-4 interviews, background checks, one week to decide

cards.front: What is the multiple hurdles approach?
cards.answer: Candidates must pass each assessment satisfactorily to advance to the next.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.16 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.16 Choosing Whom to Hire
points: Use when a minimum level is essential (firefighter strength test)
Slower and costlier

cards.front: What is the compensatory approach?
cards.answer: Combining scores so high scores on some assessments offset low scores on others.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.16 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.16 Choosing Whom to Hire
points: Strong experience can make up for a lower GPA
Not for must-have minimums

cards.front: What is a cut score?
cards.answer: The minimum score a candidate needs to be hired, set by job experts or statistics.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.16 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.16 Choosing Whom to Hire
points: High for 'hire only the best'; lower for urgent fills or cost leadership

cards.front: What is rank ordering, and its limitation?
cards.answer: Listing candidates from highest to lowest score; it doesn't guarantee they meet minimum standards.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.16 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.16 Choosing Whom to Hire
points: Pair it with a cut score

cards.front: What is the recommended final-choice practice?
cards.answer: Offer the job to the highest-ranked candidates above the cut score, with at least one backup.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.16 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.16 Choosing Whom to Hire
points: Set cut scores high enough to ensure minimum performance

cards.front: What is the employee value proposition?
cards.answer: The intrinsic and extrinsic rewards someone receives in exchange for their time and talent.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.17 Making the Job Offer
points: Maximize it, not just salary; tailor it to the finalist
Google and SAS pay average but offer standout perks

cards.front: What five categories of factors shape a job offer?
cards.answer: Job type, organizational factors, finalist factors, external factors, and legal factors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.17 Making the Job Offer
points: Organizational: policies, internal equity, urgency, union contracts, strategy
External: labor market, cost of living, competitor pay

cards.front: Why must offers respect internal equity?
cards.answer: Paying new hires more than current staff can backfire when incumbents demand matching pay.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.17 Making the Job Offer
points: An organizational factor in offer content

cards.front: What is distributive fairness in hiring?
cards.answer: The perceived fairness of the outcome, such as who got the job.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions
points: Usually low for most applicants, since most aren't hired

cards.front: What is procedural fairness in hiring?
cards.answer: The perceived fairness of the policies and procedures used to make the decision.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions
points: Driven by job relatedness, a chance to show abilities, proper questions
Violated by a hidden favorite or an illegal question

cards.front: What is interactional fairness in hiring?
cards.answer: The perceived respect and quality of interpersonal treatment candidates receive.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions
points: Violated by rude or unprepared interviewers and last-minute cancellations

cards.front: What three things drive perceptions of procedural fairness?
cards.answer: Job relatedness of the assessment, a chance to demonstrate abilities, and appropriate questions.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions
points: Candidates prefer definitive, non-invasive, validated methods

cards.front: How can an employer promote fairness in hiring?
cards.answer: Use job-related structured methods for all, let candidates show skills, and treat everyone with respect.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions; 6.6 Ethics, Legal Compliance, and Positive Stakeholder Reactions
points: Same rubric for everyone; trained interviewers; no improper questions
Explain the process; communicate promptly, including rejections
Monitor results for adverse impact

cards.front: Why does fairness still matter for rejected applicants?
cards.answer: Fair procedures and respectful treatment soften negative reactions to rejection.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions
points: Affects recommendations, buying from the firm, and lawsuit intentions

cards.front: How negotiable are job offers, per the text?
cards.answer: It varies by job, manager, organization, and candidate value; government jobs usually use fixed scales.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.19 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.19 Negotiating Employment Contracts
points: Erratum: book says mid-level ranges are 10-20% negotiable
But its example ($40K-$60K on a $50K job) is ±20%, a 40% spread

cards.front: What is a BATNA?
cards.answer: Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement; decline any offer worse than it.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.19 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.19 Negotiating Employment Contracts
points: Signaling willingness to walk away can loosen talks

cards.front: What does research show about gender and salary negotiation?
cards.answer: Far fewer women negotiate (12% vs. 52% of men in one MBA study), compounding pay gaps.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.19 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.19 Negotiating Employment Contracts
points: Negotiators gained 7-8%
Not negotiating can cost $500K+ over a career

cards.front: What is an implicit employment contract?
cards.answer: An understanding of employment terms that isn't in a written or verbal contract; the norm for most jobs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.20 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.20 The Employment Contract
points: Written contracts are more common at senior levels
A letter of agreement often substitutes

cards.front: What three elements make an employment contract legally binding?
cards.answer: Offer, acceptance, and consideration.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.20 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.20 The Employment Contract
points: Offer: clear terms
Acceptance: exactly as offered
Consideration: exchange of value, usually pay for labor

cards.front: What happens if a candidate 'accepts' but asks for $10,000 more?
cards.answer: It isn't an acceptance; adding terms makes it a counteroffer.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.20 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.20 The Employment Contract
points: Acceptance must match the offer exactly

cards.front: What is succession management in this chapter?
cards.answer: Identifying critical jobs that can't be left vacant and planning to fill them quickly.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.21 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.21 Succession Management
points: Only 30% of family businesses reach the 2nd generation
Assess potential, not just current performance

cards.front: What is Zappos's two-step hiring process?
cards.answer: First assess skills and experience for job fit, then a second interview on values for culture fit.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.22 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.22 Real World Response: How Zappos Hires the Right People
points: Rejects talented but egotistical candidates
Shuttle drivers report how candidates behave

cards.front: Why does Zappos offer new hires $3,000 to quit after training?
cards.answer: So people who don't fit the culture leave early; about 10% take the offer.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.22 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.22 Real World Response: How Zappos Hires the Right People
points: Follows a 4-week paid training on culture and customer obsession

cards.front: What is open hiring at The Body Shop?
cards.answer: Hiring first-come, first-served after three yes/no questions, with no interview, background check, or drug test.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.23 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.23 Strategic HRM Exercise: Open Hiring at the Body Shop
points: Authorized to work? Stand 8 hours? Lift 50+ lbs?
Monthly turnover fell 60%

cards.front: What is reliability?
cards.answer: Consistency: a measure gives similar scores when repeated.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.25 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.25 Appendix: Reliability and Validity
points: Coefficient 0-1: above 0.70 acceptable, 0.80+ preferred
Necessary but not sufficient

cards.front: What is validity?
cards.answer: How well a measure assesses what it claims and predicts what matters, such as job success.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.25 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.25 Appendix: Reliability and Validity
points: Specific to a purpose and to a group
UGESP requires evidence if a tool has adverse impact

cards.front: Can an unreliable measure be valid?
cards.answer: No. Reliability is necessary for validity, though a reliable measure can still be invalid.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.25 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.25 Appendix: Reliability and Validity
points: Height is reliable but not valid for most jobs
Target: tight cluster = reliable; centered = valid

cards.front: Priya, interviewing for a nurse-manager role, is asked: "Tell me about a time you had to correct a coworker's charting error. What did you do, and what happened?" Which interview type is this?
cards.explanation: It asks about a real past event (situation, action, result), so it's behavioral. Past behavior predicts future behavior.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: A bank asks a recent graduate: "Suppose a customer insists on withdrawing cash without ID and starts shouting. How would you handle it?" Which interview type is this?
cards.explanation: A hypothetical 'how would you handle' question is situational. It suits candidates with limited experience.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: A consulting firm hands Marcus a one-page brief, "A regional grocer's profits fell 12% last year," and asks him to talk through how he'd diagnose and fix it. Which interview type is this?
cards.explanation: Solving a business problem aloud is a case interview. The reasoning process matters more than the final answer.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Every candidate for a dispatcher job answers the same six questions drawn from a job analysis, and two trained raters score each answer against a 1-5 key. What kind of interview is this?
cards.explanation: Same questions, built from job analysis, with a formal scoring key: the three features of a structured interview.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: A store manager chats with each applicant about whatever comes up, then hires the one who "felt right." What's the main problem with this approach?
choices: It's a situational interview: too focused on hypotheticals
It's an unstructured interview: inconsistent and a weak predictor
It's a case interview: too focused on business problems
It's a behavioral interview: too focused on past events
cards.explanation: Varying questions with no answer standards define an unstructured interview, which predicts poorly (0.20-0.38) and is legally risky.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: A hiring manager is filling an entry-level role. Most applicants are students with little work history. Which structured interview type fits best?
choices: Behavioral, because it relies on candidates' past jobs
Unstructured, because students need a relaxed chat
Case, because every role needs a business problem to solve
Situational, because it doesn't require past examples
cards.explanation: Situational questions pose hypotheticals, so they work for candidates without relevant past experience.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: For a senior project manager opening, the panel wants evidence of how candidates actually led troubled projects. Which interview type fits best?
cards.explanation: Behavioral interviews ask experienced candidates to describe real situations, actions, and results.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: "If you were assigned to a team that disagreed with your approach, what would you do?" Which interview type is this?
cards.explanation: 'What would you do' is a hypothetical, so it's situational. Rephrased as 'Tell me about a time a team disagreed with you,' it would be behavioral.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Jae is asked to estimate how many electric-scooter chargers a mid-size city needs and explain his assumptions out loud. What is the interviewer mainly assessing?
choices: His personality fit with the team
Whether he gets the exact right number
cards.explanation: Case interviews rarely have one right answer. They assess business reasoning, presentation, and communication, so thinking aloud matters.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Two interviewers ask candidates for the same job completely different questions and rate them on gut feel. What fix would improve both fairness and prediction most?
choices: Longer interviews so the gut feel is surer
Letting each interviewer pick favorite questions
Adding a third interviewer who also uses gut feel
Same job-based questions with a scoring key
cards.explanation: Structuring the interview (same questions, job analysis, formal scoring) raises validity to 0.51-0.63 and makes the process procedurally fair.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: After Lena's final interview, the recruiter calls to explain she wasn't chosen, answers her questions, and thanks her for her time. Fair or unfair, and which type?
cards.explanation: Respectful, considerate treatment during a rejection upholds interactional fairness.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: Omar posts the top score on a validated skills test, but the manager rejects him because she "just had a bad feeling." Fair or unfair, and which type?
cards.explanation: Ignoring the established, job-related process in favor of a gut feeling violates procedural fairness.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: A firm scores every candidate with the same interview rubric so each is judged on identical criteria. Fair or unfair, and which type?
cards.explanation: Consistent, job-related procedures applied to everyone uphold procedural fairness.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: Aisha is hired because she's the most qualified candidate, even though another finalist is the manager's golf buddy. Fair or unfair, and which type?
cards.explanation: The outcome went to the most deserving candidate, so distributive (outcome) fairness is upheld.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: An interviewer shows up 25 minutes late, checks his phone throughout, and cuts the candidate off mid-answer. Which fairness type is violated?
cards.explanation: Rude, disrespectful treatment violates interactional fairness, regardless of the procedures or outcome.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: Carlos learns the job was promised to an internal favorite before interviews began, and he never got to show his skills. Which fairness type is violated?
cards.explanation: A rigged process with no chance to demonstrate abilities violates procedural fairness (the book's 'Judy' example).
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: The manager's nephew, who failed two required certifications, gets the job over three qualified finalists. Which fairness type is most directly violated?
cards.explanation: The outcome went to an undeserving person, violating distributive (outcome) fairness. The favoritism also raises procedural concerns.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: An interviewer asks a candidate whether she plans to have children soon. Which fairness type does this question damage most?
choices: Interactional, but only if she ends up rejected
None, since asking about family plans is fine
Distributive, through an unfair hiring outcome
cards.explanation: Improper or illegal questions undermine procedural fairness, and family plans aren't job-related.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: A firm can't hire most of its 400 applicants. What would most improve how rejected applicants view it?
choices: Rejecting everyone at once by a form letter months later
Clear, job-related steps and courteous, timely rejections
Hiring more people than needed to raise distributive fairness
Saying nothing so no one can complain about the reason
cards.explanation: Distributive fairness will be low for most applicants anyway; procedural and interactional fairness soften the reaction to rejection.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: HR wants to make its hiring fairer. Which change does NOT promote fairness?
choices: Telling candidates the steps and timeline up front
Letting each manager use personal favorite questions
Basing every assessment on a job analysis
Training interviewers and using a common scoring key
cards.explanation: Inconsistent, manager-chosen questions undermine procedural fairness; the other three promote it.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: Brightline Labs prizes experimentation and candor. Candidate Nia describes loving rapid testing and blunt feedback, and the interviewer notes, "She thinks the way we work." What does this show?
choices: Her values and work style align with the culture
Her technical skills meet the job's requirements
She'll mesh well with her immediate supervisor
Her pay expectations fit the salary range
cards.explanation: Matching personal values and work style to organizational culture and norms is person-organization fit.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: A nonprofit hires Diego because his commitment to community service matches its mission and values. Which kind of fit was assessed?
cards.explanation: Values aligning with the organization's mission and culture is P-O fit.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: An airline confirms Mei's certifications and flight hours meet the first-officer requirements. Which kind of fit is this?
cards.explanation: Matching abilities and qualifications to job demands is person-job fit, the primary focus of most assessment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: A six-person design team works on every project together. Before hiring, they meet each finalist to judge communication style and how the person handles conflict. Which fit are they assessing?
cards.explanation: Fit with coworkers and the supervisor is person-group fit, which matters most when work is interdependent.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: Raj wants flexible hours and project variety; the role offers both, plus the pay he needs. Which fit does this describe?
choices: Person-job: his needs match the job's rewards
cards.explanation: Person-job fit includes needs and motivations matching the job's attributes and rewards, not just ability matching demands.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: A firm hires mostly for culture fit. What outcome should it expect P-O fit to improve most?
choices: Cognitive test scores on future assessments
Speed of learning complex new tasks
Satisfaction, commitment, and intent to stay
cards.explanation: P-O fit strongly predicts attitudes and retention but has little effect on meeting job requirements, so pair it with person-job assessment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: A manager says, "For culture fit, I hire people who went to my college and share my hobbies." What's the problem?
choices: Nothing; shared hobbies are the core of P-O fit
It measures person-job fit, not culture fit
It's fine as long as the questions are structured
That's similarity, not fit, and risks discrimination
cards.explanation: Hiring for fit isn't hiring people you're comfortable with. Fit should be defined by job-related values, or it slides into stereotyping.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: A resort asks housekeeping applicants, "What does a truly clean room mean to you?" and screens for warmth before teaching skills. Whose approach is this modeled on, and what fit?
choices: Zappos, screening for job knowledge first
MITRE, screening for technical skills first
Body Shop, hiring with no screening at all
Hilton, screening for culture fit first
cards.explanation: Hilton screens first for brand and culture fit (hospitality as a calling) and trains skills later.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.5 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: A software company wants to protect its collaborative culture without sacrificing skills. Which process mirrors Zappos?
choices: Assess values only and skip skills entirely
Assess skills only and let culture sort itself out
Hire everyone and fire whoever doesn't fit
Assess skills first, then values in a second interview
cards.explanation: Zappos uses two steps: job fit (skills, experience), then culture fit (attitudes, values, personality).
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.22 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.22 Real World Response: How Zappos Hires the Right People

cards.front: A hospital hires a surgeon who later causes several serious errors. Which selection outcome is this?
cards.explanation: Hired but unsuccessful is a false positive, the costliest error in high-risk jobs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.4 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.4 Assessment Goals

cards.front: A tech firm rejects a programmer who joins a rival and builds its best-selling product. Which outcome is this?
cards.explanation: Rejected but would have succeeded is a false negative, costly when talent strengthens a competitor.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.4 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.4 Assessment Goals

cards.front: After a contingent offer, a delivery company runs a drug screen and a driving-record check. Which kind of assessment is this?
cards.explanation: Checks run after a contingent offer, where passing leads to the final offer, are contingent methods.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.7 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.7 Assessment Methods

cards.front: A recruiter reviews 600 applications to find the 40 who meet minimum requirements. Which kind of method is she using?
cards.explanation: Screening methods narrow applicants down to candidates against minimum qualifications.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.7 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.7 Assessment Methods

cards.front: The 40 remaining candidates take a job simulation and a structured interview so the firm can decide whom to hire. What kind of methods are these?
cards.explanation: In-depth tools used to decide whom to hire are evaluative methods.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.7 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.7 Assessment Methods

cards.front: A manager wants every applicant to take a medical exam on day one, before interviews. What's the problem?
choices: Medical exams can only be given to current employees
Medical exams are allowed only for executive-level roles
Nothing; earlier exams save everyone time
Medical exams must wait until after a contingent offer
cards.explanation: Under the ADA, medical exams come only after a contingent offer and must be given to everyone entering the job.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.13 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.13 Contingent Assessment Methods: Reference Checks and Medical and Drug Tests

cards.front: To be hired as firefighters, candidates must first pass a strength test, then a written test, then an interview, failing out at any step. Which approach is this?
cards.explanation: Having to pass each assessment to advance is multiple hurdles, used when a minimum level is essential.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.16 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.16 Choosing Whom to Hire

cards.front: A school lets a teacher candidate's outstanding classroom demo make up for a mediocre written exam. Which approach is this?
cards.explanation: Letting high scores offset low ones is the compensatory approach.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.16 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.16 Choosing Whom to Hire

cards.front: A pharmacy must ensure every hire can count medications with zero errors, but other skills can trade off. Which design fits best?
choices: Compensatory scoring for all skills, accuracy included
Rank ordering with no minimum score set
A hurdle for accuracy, then compensatory scoring
cards.explanation: Use a hurdle for must-have minimums, then let the remaining scores compensate for one another.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.16 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.16 Choosing Whom to Hire

cards.front: HR ranks 12 finalists by total score. The top three all fall below the minimum acceptable score. What should HR do?
choices: Average the top three into a single hire
Lower the job's requirements to fit them
Offer only to candidates above the cut score
Offer to the top three because they ranked first
cards.explanation: Rank ordering doesn't guarantee minimum standards. Best practice is the highest-ranked candidates who are above the cut score.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.16 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.16 Choosing Whom to Hire

cards.front: A low-cost retailer needs to fill 200 seasonal jobs within two weeks. How should its cut score compare to a firm that hires 'only the best'?
choices: Identical, since cut scores never vary
No cut score at all, just rank ordering
Lower, to fit urgency and target pay
Higher, to make up for the rushed timeline
cards.explanation: Cut scores reflect strategy: urgent fills and cost leadership use lower cut scores; 'hire only the best' uses higher ones.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.16 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.16 Choosing Whom to Hire

cards.front: A firm wants the single best predictor of performance for complex analyst roles at moderate cost. Which choice does Table 6.3 support?
choices: A personality test used by itself
A structured interview or cognitive test
An unstructured interview by the CEO
cards.explanation: Structured interviews (0.51-0.63) and cognitive tests (0.51) top the table; unstructured interviews and references are among the weakest.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.7 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.7 Assessment Methods

cards.front: A city uses only a cognitive ability test to hire, and pass rates differ sharply by race. What's the best fix?
choices: Combine it with other valid assessments
Drop all testing and interview on gut feel
Keep it as the only tool; it's highly valid
Raise the cut score to screen out more people
cards.explanation: Cognitive tests predict well but tend to cause disparate impact. Combining them with other tools reduces adverse impact while keeping prediction.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.9 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.9 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Cognitive and Noncognitive Ability Tests

cards.front: A jewelry store wants a cheap test that predicts theft, adds to its cognitive test, and has little adverse impact. Which fits?
cards.explanation: Integrity tests are inexpensive, predict theft and counterproductive behavior, have low adverse impact, and are unrelated to cognitive ability.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.10 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.10 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Personality and Values Assessments and Integrity Tests

cards.front: A company wants one personality trait that predicts performance across all its very different jobs. Which should it measure?
cards.explanation: Conscientiousness predicts performance in all occupations; the others predict only specific jobs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.10 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.10 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Personality and Values Assessments and Integrity Tests

cards.front: A 911 center has applicants handle recorded mock emergency calls while being scored. What method is this?
cards.explanation: Giving real tasks or recreating critical job events is a simulation, a type of work sample (validity 0.54).
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.12 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.12 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Work Samples and Interviews (Work Samples & Assessment Centers)

cards.front: Six management candidates spend two days handling an in-basket, leading a group discussion, and presenting, while trained raters rotate observing. What is this?
cards.explanation: A battery of exercises scored by multiple trained assessors is an assessment center.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.12 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.12 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Work Samples and Interviews (Work Samples & Assessment Centers)

cards.front: A firm's Table 6.3 copy lists job knowledge test validity as .048, and a manager concludes the tests are useless. What's the right response?
choices: It means they predict only 48% of hires
It's 4.8, the highest value in the table
It's a typo for 0.48, a good predictor
Correct; .048 means the tests don't predict
cards.explanation: Erratum: the book prints '.048', but the validity is 0.48. Job knowledge tests predict well, especially for complex jobs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: A bathroom scale shows 150, 162, and 141 lb for the same person within one minute. What's wrong, and can it be valid?
choices: It's valid as long as the average is right
It's reliable because it gives numbers
It's unreliable, so it can't be valid
It's reliable but simply not valid
cards.explanation: Wildly inconsistent results mean low reliability, and an unreliable measure cannot be valid.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.25 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.25 Appendix: Reliability and Validity

cards.front: A test gives very consistent scores but doesn't predict who succeeds on the job. How would you describe it?
cards.explanation: Consistency (reliability) is necessary but not sufficient; prediction for the purpose is validity. Height is reliable but not valid.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.25 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.25 Appendix: Reliability and Validity

cards.front: A background check turns up a negative credit item that will cost Tanya the offer. What must the employer give her?
choices: A copy of other applicants' reports
An adverse action notice and the right to dispute
cards.explanation: Under the FCRA process, she gets the report, the screener's contact information, and fair time to dispute errors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.14 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.14 Contingent Assessment Methods: Background Checks

cards.front: A state contractor's application asks, "Have you ever been convicted of a crime?" before anyone is screened. Which kind of law targets this practice?
cards.explanation: Ban-the-box laws delay criminal-history questions until after initial qualification (federal: after a conditional offer).
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.14 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.14 Contingent Assessment Methods: Background Checks

cards.front: A startup can't match a bank's salary, so it highlights equity, remote work, and fast skill growth. What is it maximizing?
cards.explanation: The employee value proposition is the full mix of intrinsic and extrinsic rewards, not just salary.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.17 Making the Job Offer

cards.front: A manager wants to offer a new hire $15K more than three current team members doing the same job. Which offer factor is at risk?
choices: Labor market tightness, an external factor
cards.explanation: Internal equity is an organizational factor; above-market new-hire pay can backfire when incumbents demand matching.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.17 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.17 Making the Job Offer

cards.front: Kim's other offer pays $72K. Her preferred employer stops at $68K with no other perks. Using BATNA logic, what should she do?
choices: Ignore the other offer when deciding
Take the $72K offer, since it beats this one
Keep negotiating forever until they say yes
cards.explanation: Your BATNA is your best alternative; decline offers worse than it (assuming pay is what matters most to her).
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.19 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.19 Negotiating Employment Contracts

cards.front: An employer offers Ben $80K; he replies, "I accept at $85K." What is the legal status?
cards.explanation: Acceptance must match the offer exactly; adding terms makes it a counteroffer.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.20 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 6.20 The Employment Contract

cards.front: A small bakery owner tells a new baker, "You'll work mornings and get $18 an hour," with nothing written. What kind of contract is this?
choices: A written contract under the FCRA
An implicit contract, the norm for most jobs
An invalid arrangement with no legal effect
cards.explanation: Most jobs run on an implicit employment contract, an understanding not formalized in a written contract.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.20 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.20 The Employment Contract

cards.front: A $60K-midpoint job's range is $48K-$72K. Using the book's own example as the model, how is the range described?
cards.explanation: The book's example ($40K-$60K on $50K) is ±20%; this range follows the same pattern. Note the book's text says 10-20%, which its example contradicts.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.19 Apply · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.19 Negotiating Employment Contracts

cards.front: Most hiring assessment focuses primarily on which kind of fit?
cards.explanation: Person-job fit is the primary focus because it drives performance.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.5 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: When employees' work is highly interdependent, which fit becomes most important?
cards.explanation: Person-group fit matters most in interdependent work such as teams.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.5 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: Per the text's wording, which fit influences satisfaction, performance, commitment, and retention?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: person-organization fit. Moderate confidence: the same section says P-O fit has little effect on meeting job requirements, so 'performance' is loose wording. Its strong links are satisfaction, commitment, and intent to stay.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.5 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: A candidate who passes a background check, drug screen, and medical exam receives a formal offer. Those checks are which kind of assessment?
cards.explanation: Contingent methods follow a contingent offer; passing leads to the formal offer.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.7 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.7 Assessment Methods

cards.front: Which methods narrow the applicant pool down to candidates?
cards.explanation: Screening methods check minimum qualifications to turn applicants into candidates.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.7 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.7 Assessment Methods

cards.front: Which methods are used to decide whom to hire from among candidates?
cards.explanation: Evaluative methods assess candidates in depth to choose hires.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.7 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.7 Assessment Methods

cards.front: Which interview is inconsistent across candidates and makes answers hard to compare?
cards.explanation: Unstructured interviews vary questions and lack answer standards.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Which interview type assumes that past actions predict future behavior?
cards.explanation: Behavioral interviews ask about real past situations, actions, and results.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: "How would you handle a conflict with a customer?" is an example of which interview type?
cards.explanation: A hypothetical 'how would you' question is situational.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Which interview uses the same questions for everyone and a scoring system?
cards.explanation: Same questions plus formal scoring define a structured interview.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.11 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Which kind of work sample gives applicants real tasks or recreates critical job events?
cards.explanation: Simulations present real tasks or critical events.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.12 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.12 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Work Samples and Interviews (Work Samples & Assessment Centers)

cards.front: Fairness of hiring outcomes is called...
cards.explanation: Distributive fairness concerns outcomes.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: Fairness of hiring policies and procedures is called...
cards.explanation: Procedural fairness concerns the process.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: Rude or unprepared interviewers damage which kind of fairness?
cards.explanation: Interactional fairness concerns respectful interpersonal treatment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6.18 Practice · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: Sometimes ___ a poor fit is worth more than ___ good performers.
cards.explanation: Likely per text: not hiring a poor fit can be worth more than hiring good performers, because one bad hire can do great damage.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q1 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.4 Assessment Goals

cards.front: Fit between a person's desires and motivations and a job's attributes and rewards is...
cards.explanation: Likely per text: person-job fit covers both abilities vs. demands and needs vs. rewards.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q2 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: The match between a person and their workgroup and supervisor is...
cards.explanation: Likely per text: person-group fit includes coworkers and the supervisor.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q3 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: The match between a person's values, attitudes, and personality and an organization's values, norms, and culture is...
cards.explanation: Likely per text: that's the definition of P-O fit.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q4 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: Which fit is based partly on a person's motivations matching the job's rewards?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: person-job fit includes needs and motivations vs. job rewards.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q5 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: Which type of fit includes the relationship with one's supervisor?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: person-group fit covers the workgroup and supervisor.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q6 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.5 Fit

cards.front: Which interview asks candidates different questions with no standard for evaluating answers?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: unstructured interviews vary questions and lack answer standards.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q7 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Which interview uses consistent, job-related questions with predetermined scoring keys?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: structured interviews use the same job-based questions and formal scoring.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q8 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Which interview type is not recommended because of its expense and legal risk?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: unstructured interviews are costly, legally risky, and weak predictors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q9 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Which interview presents a hypothetical scenario and asks how the candidate would react?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: hypotheticals define situational interviews.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q10 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Well-developed ___ interviews are good predictors of job performance.
cards.explanation: Likely per text: structured. Moderate confidence: situational and behavioral interviews are both types of structured interview and also predict well, but the text's general statement is about structured interviews.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q11 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: "Tell me about a time you had to write up an employee" is from which interview type?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: 'tell me about a time' asks about past behavior, so behavioral.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q12 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: In which interview does the candidate get a business problem and present a solution?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: that's a case interview.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q13 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Which interview assesses business knowledge, reasoning, and presentation skills and is common in consulting and banking?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: case interviews.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q14 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.11 Evaluative Assessment Methods: Job Knowledge Tests and Interviews

cards.front: Perceived respect and quality of interpersonal treatment is which type of fairness?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: interactional fairness.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q15 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: Judy thinks the manager had a favorite all along, and she never got a chance to show her skills. Which fairness is in question?
cards.explanation: Likely per text: a biased process with no chance to demonstrate abilities is procedural unfairness.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q16 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: Rude interviewers, last-minute cancellations, and an unhelpful negotiator signal low ___ fairness.
cards.explanation: Likely per text: interactional fairness.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q17 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions

cards.front: Because most applicants don't get the job, ___ fairness is often low.
cards.explanation: Likely per text: distributive (outcome) fairness.
cards.subtitle: Ch 6 Quiz Q18 · Effective HRM
cards.note: Read more: 6.18 Fairness Perceptions
